I'd like to add more details about the empty issue you discussed during the latest community call. There are many cloud providers that do not have a metadata service. In such environments, the VM bootstrap script cannot set the correctly, so the kubelet joins the cluster without this information. The CCM then needs to identify the node using its hostname, internal IP address, or system UUID and resolve the corresponding through the cloud provider API. My proposal to introduce the flag aims to address these cases by giving the CCM more time to initialize the node before the node lifecycle controller starts discover the node too. It could also help reduce unnecessary API calls during the node join and initialization process, especially when many nodes join the cluster at the same time. I also remember trying to address a similar issue a few years ago in this PR: http in OpenStack CCM - 100 nodes scale up -> 4500 cloud API calls in ~5 second

One reservation I have from the build backend side of things is that it's not fully clear to me how to wire this up while at the same time allowing users to choose. My understanding from the PEP is that this is "just" about ensuring that globally distributed binaries (Linux distro packages, conda, cibuildwheel outputs published to PyPI, etc.) don't hinder adoption for users that need to do tracing. These "good defaults" should therefore be getting applied when building redistributable wheels. Ideally we'd have some mechanism for determining when a wheel is intended for redistribution. There's currently no real way to know this, other than I guess "groups doing distribution at scale usually set CFLAGS themselves". Relatedly, what should complex compiled projects do when they have internal libraries of e.g. scientific code that get built as a static library, and then linked into python bindings? The vast bulk of the code isn't a python extension and isn't built with any cpython flags whatsoever. Only the binding code is. So you get frame pointers for the binding code but immediately hit a dead end because the implementation is missing them... In meson it is generally recommended for target cleanliness to logically group compilation units by purpose, and often that will be a "subproject" which you don't even develop yourself, but rather use via a git submodule. None of it uses Python.h and the upstream build definitions (which are directly invoked in a subproject build) don't link to the python dependency (and are probably created by people who don't know python at all). It is "just" a C++ static library. Where should these flags be added?

I've been investigating this issue and have developed a prototype optimisation for "np.isin" on "dtype=object" arrays, including arrays containing ordinary Python objects. Proposed approach The implementation uses a hash-based fast path for supported object types, falling back to NumPy's existing comparison-based implementation when necessary. I've experimented with: - Built-in Python integers and strings. - Unhashable built-in containers, including lists and dictionaries. - Custom hashable Python classes. - Handling NaNs, hash collisions, and unusual equality behaviour. The fastest version uses a small C implementation to avoid per-element Python overhead. Preliminary benchmarks Measured on Linux with NumPy 2.3.5: Workload| NumPy| Prototype| Speedup 100k Python integer objects| 789 ms| 2.38 ms| 332× 100k Python string objects| 1,317 ms| 2.06 ms| 639× 30k Python lists| 217 ms| 4.77 ms| 45× 30k Python dictionaries| 299 ms| 11.2 ms| 27× I ran correctness tests covering NaNs, unhashable objects, hash collisions, mixed types, custom equality methods, and non-contiguous arrays. Questions for maintainers Before preparing a PR, I'd appreciate feedback on the following: 1. Would a hash-based fast path restricted to supported built-in Python types be acceptable? 2. Would you prefer a smaller Python-only optimisation initially, or a C implementation offering substantially larger speedups? 3. Would there be interest in extending the optimisation to arbitrary hashable Python objects, potentially as a separate change? I'm happy to share the prototype, benchmark code, and tests.
